text: Shebang purpose → picks the interpreter → `#!/usr/bin/env bash` finds bash in `PATH`
title: Bash Basics

text: `$@` vs `$*` → `"$@"` keeps each arg separate, `"$*"` glues them into one string
title: Bash Basics

text: Why is `cd` a builtin → a separate program can't change your shell's directory
title: Bash Basics

text: `a=5; a+=2` gives `52` → variables are strings → use `$(( ))` for math
title: Bash Basics

text: `[` vs `[[` → `[` is a command with word splitting, `[[` is a keyword without it
title: Conditionals, Loops & Functions

text: `a && b || c` → `c` also runs if `b` fails → not a real if/else
title: Conditionals, Loops & Functions

text: `return` vs `exit` → `return` ends the function, `exit` ends the whole script
title: Conditionals, Loops & Functions

text: Why never `for f in $(ls)` → filenames with spaces split → use `for f in *`
title: Conditionals, Loops & Functions

text: `set -euo pipefail` flag by flag → `-e` stop on failure, `-u` error on unset var, `-o pipefail` pipe fails if any part fails
title: Script Safety

text: Does `set -e` catch everything → no, not inside `if` or before `&&` `||` → safety net, not guarantee
title: Script Safety

text: `trap cleanup EXIT` → cleanup runs even when the script fails
title: Script Safety

text: Common bash pitfalls → quote vars, globs not `ls`, handle failures
title: Script Safety

text: What does the docker CLI do? → nothing by itself; it sends REST API requests to dockerd over /var/run/docker.sock
title: Architecture

text: Why is access to docker.sock dangerous? → whoever can write to it controls dockerd, which runs as root, so it is effectively root access
title: Architecture

text: dockerd vs containerd? → dockerd handles Docker features (API, builds, networks, volumes, logs); containerd only manages images and container lifecycle
title: Architecture

text: What does runc do? → creates namespaces and cgroups, sets the root filesystem, starts the process, then exits
title: Architecture

text: Why a shim per container? → it stays as the container's parent, keeps its logs and exit code, so dockerd/containerd can restart without killing containers
title: Architecture

text: Does Kubernetes need Docker? → no, it talks to containerd directly
title: Architecture

text: What is a daemon? → a background program that runs all the time waiting for work, usually named with a trailing d
title: Architecture

text: Why does a container exit immediately? → its main process ended; e.g. bash with no terminal exits at once
title: Containers

text: docker stop vs docker kill? → stop sends SIGTERM, waits 10s, then SIGKILL; kill sends SIGKILL immediately
title: Containers

text: Is a stopped container deleted? → no, it stays with its writable layer until docker rm
title: Containers

text: What does --rm do? → deletes the container automatically when it stops; it does not remove a running container
title: Containers

text: docker run vs docker start? → run creates a new container; start restarts an existing stopped one
title: Containers

text: docker run vs docker exec? → run makes a new container; exec runs a command inside an existing running one
title: Containers

text: docker ps -aq? → IDs of all containers, running and stopped, used with $( ) to feed other commands
title: Containers

text: docker rm vs docker rmi? → rm removes containers, rmi removes images
title: Containers

text: Exit code 143? → the process got SIGTERM
title: Containers

text: What is the Docker socket? → `/var/run/docker.sock`, the Unix socket the daemon listens on. The CLI and tools like Portainer use the REST API through it
title: The Docker Socket

text: Why is mounting it dangerous? → the daemon runs as root, so a process with the socket can start a container with the host's `/` mounted. It is root on the host
title: The Docker Socket

text: Does `--network none` protect a container that has the socket? → no, the socket is a file mount, not a network path
title: The Docker Socket

text: Why do CI runners mount it? → to start sibling containers on the host's daemon (Docker-out-of-Docker). Docker-in-Docker runs its own daemon in a privileged container instead
title: The Docker Socket

text: How do you make socket access safer? → rootless Docker or Podman, a socket proxy that allows only certain API calls, no mount into untrusted containers
title: The Docker Socket

text: Why is `docker` group membership a security concern? → it can reach the socket, which is equivalent to root
title: The Docker Socket

text: Why is exposing the daemon on TCP `2375` bad? → no TLS or auth, anyone on the network gets root. If you need remote access use `2376` with TLS
title: The Docker Socket

text: Why did Portainer show 0 containers on a newer Docker? → the daemon raised its minimum API version and an old Portainer client was rejected, so upgrade Portainer
title: The Docker Socket

text: Which two mounts does a Portainer container need and why? → the socket (bind mount, to control Docker) and a volume on `/data` (to keep its settings)
title: The Docker Socket

text: Dockerfile vs image vs container? → the Dockerfile is the instructions, the image is what they build, a container is a running instance of the image
title: Dockerfile

text: `RUN` vs `CMD`? → `RUN` executes at build time and saves a layer, `CMD` is stored in the image and executes each time a container starts
title: Dockerfile

text: `CMD` vs `ENTRYPOINT`? → `ENTRYPOINT` is the fixed executable, `CMD` supplies default arguments and is easy to override with `docker run`
title: Dockerfile

text: `ARG` vs `ENV`? → `ARG` exists only during the build, `ENV` is also set in running containers
title: Dockerfile

text: Why does `docker run --build-arg` fail? → `--build-arg` is a `docker build` option, `ARG` values are fixed once the image is built
title: Dockerfile

text: Why does nginx need `daemon off;`? → a container stops when its main process exits, and nginx backgrounds itself by default
title: Dockerfile

text: Exec form vs shell form of `CMD`? → exec form runs the program directly as the main process, shell form wraps it in `/bin/sh -c`
title: Dockerfile

text: Does `EXPOSE` publish a port? → no, it only documents it, `-p` publishes it
title: Dockerfile

text: `COPY` vs `ADD`? → `ADD` also extracts archives and downloads URLs, `COPY` is simpler and preferred
title: Dockerfile

text: What does `.dockerignore` do? → keeps files like `.git` and `.env` out of the build context so they are not sent to the daemon or copied in
title: Dockerfile

text: `CMD` vs `ENTRYPOINT`? → `ENTRYPOINT` is the fixed executable, `CMD` is the default command or arguments and is replaced by anything after the image name in `docker run`
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: Both in one Dockerfile? → `CMD` is passed as arguments to `ENTRYPOINT`, so the image behaves like a command with default flags
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: How do you override `ENTRYPOINT`? → `docker run --entrypoint cmd image`, in Kubernetes the `command` field
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: Why use exec form? → the program is PID 1 and receives `SIGTERM` from `docker stop`, shell form puts `/bin/sh -c` in front and the signal may never reach the app
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: A container starts and exits immediately, why? → its main process finished or ran in the background, keep it in the foreground, for nginx `daemon off;`
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: `docker run app ping host` fails on an image with `ENTRYPOINT ["ping"]`, why? → the extra `ping` is appended as an argument and read as a hostname
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: Where are `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD` visible? → `docker inspect` shows `Path`, `Args`, `Config.Entrypoint` and `Config.Cmd`
title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD

text: Does `EXPOSE` publish a port? → no, it documents it, `-p` publishes, `-P` publishes all `EXPOSE`d ports to random host ports
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: `EXPOSE 80` and `-p 8000:8000`, what happens? → `-p` wins, host 8000 goes to container 8000, if the app listens on 80 the connection fails with no warning
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: `COPY` vs `ADD`? → `ADD` also extracts local tarballs and downloads URLs, a downloaded archive is not extracted, use `COPY` and `RUN curl` instead
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: Why `WORKDIR` instead of `RUN cd`? → `cd` lasts one `RUN`, `WORKDIR` applies to every later instruction and to the running container
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: Why run as non-root? → a breakout or a bug then gives an unprivileged user, not root
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: Build fails with `Permission denied` in `apt`, why? → `USER` was set before the install, root-only steps must run first
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: Can a non-root user run nginx on port 80? → not by default, ports below 1024 need root or a capability, use 8080
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: How do you build with a differently named Dockerfile? → `docker build -f name -t tag .`, the `.` stays the context
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: Why are secrets in `ENV` bad? → they are baked into the image layers and show up in `docker inspect` and `docker history`
title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER

text: What is an image layer? → a read-only filesystem diff made by an instruction like `RUN` or `COPY`, stacked to form the image and shared between images
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: Which instructions make the image bigger? → `RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`. `ENV`, `ARG`, `LABEL`, `CMD` are 0B metadata
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: How does the build cache work? → a layer is reused if its instruction and all earlier layers are unchanged. The first change invalidates everything below it
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: How do you order a Dockerfile for fast rebuilds? → rarely changing steps first (base, packages, dependencies), frequently changing steps (your code) last
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: Does deleting a file in a later layer reduce image size? → no, the earlier layer still holds it. Delete in the same `RUN`
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: Image ID vs tag? → the ID identifies the image content, a tag is a movable name. Rebuilding under the same tag moves the tag to a new ID
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: What is a dangling image and how do you remove it? → an untagged image left behind when a tag moves. `docker image prune`
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: What does `docker system prune` remove? → stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and unused build cache
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: Why are secrets in `ENV` bad, and what do you do instead? → they are stored in the image and visible via `docker history` and `docker inspect`. Pass them at run time or use an IAM role, and rotate any key that was baked in
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: What does `<missing>` mean in `docker history`? → those layers have no local image ID, which is normal for layers from a base image or BuildKit
title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup

text: What is an image layer? → a read-only slice of the filesystem created by RUN, COPY or ADD, identified by a content hash
title: Images & Storage

text: What is copy-on-write? → changing a file from a lower layer copies it up into the container's writable layer first; the image is never modified
title: Images & Storage

text: Why doesn't deleting a file in a later layer shrink the image? → it only adds a whiteout marker; the file still exists in the earlier layer
title: Images & Storage

text: Does latest mean newest? → no, it is just a default tag name that can point anywhere
title: Images & Storage

text: docker pull says manifest unknown for :latest? → the repo has no latest tag; pass an existing tag explicitly
title: Images & Storage

text: Tag vs digest? → tag is mutable, digest (sha256) always points to the exact same image
title: Images & Storage

text: RUN vs CMD? → RUN executes at build time; CMD is the default command each time a container starts
title: Images & Storage

text: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT? → ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable; CMD supplies default arguments that docker run can replace
title: Images & Storage

text: Does EXPOSE publish a port? → no, it only documents it; only -p publishes
title: Images & Storage

text: Why order Dockerfile instructions carefully? → a changed layer invalidates the cache for every layer after it
title: Images & Storage

text: Volume vs bind mount? → volume is managed by Docker under /var/lib/docker/volumes; bind mount maps a host path I choose
title: Images & Storage

text: Where does container data go when the container is removed? → the writable layer is deleted; only volumes and bind mounts survive
title: Images & Storage

text: How do you check how Docker was installed on Ubuntu? → dpkg -l for docker-ce vs docker.io, and snap list
title: Install & Upgrade

text: docker.io vs docker-ce? → docker.io is Ubuntu's package and lags behind; docker-ce comes from Docker's official repo
title: Install & Upgrade

text: Service shows disabled but Docker works? → socket activation: systemd starts dockerd when something connects to docker.socket
title: Install & Upgrade

text: Why is docker0 missing? → dockerd isn't running (or bridge is disabled in daemon.json); dockerd creates docker0 at startup
title: Install & Upgrade

text: enable vs start? → start runs it now, enable starts it at boot; enable --now does both
title: Install & Upgrade

text: Does removing docker.io delete my images? → no, apt remove without --purge keeps /var/lib/docker
title: Install & Upgrade

text: Container vs VM? → VM has its own kernel and full OS; container is a process sharing the host kernel, so it is smaller and starts in milliseconds but isolation is weaker
title: Introduction

text: What is a container, technically? → a normal Linux process with namespaces (what it sees), cgroups (what it uses) and a layered filesystem
title: Introduction

text: Why does a container stop when its app exits? → the container lives only as long as its main process (PID 1)
title: Introduction

text: Exit code 137? → process got SIGKILL, often the OOM killer after hitting the memory limit
title: Introduction

text: Can a Linux container run on a Windows kernel natively? → no, containers share the host kernel; Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM for this
title: Introduction

text: Image vs container? → image is the read-only template, container is a running instance of it with its own writable layer
title: Introduction

text: Where does docker logs get its data? → from /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log, written by the json-file log driver
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: How do you find a container's log file path? → docker inspect -f '{{.LogPath}}' <name>
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: Why do nginx notices appear as stderr? → nginx writes its own logs to stderr by design; it does not mean an error
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: What happens to logs when a container is removed? → the whole container folder, logs included, is deleted
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: How do you stop container logs filling the disk? → set log-opts max-size and max-file in /etc/docker/daemon.json
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: Where does a container's /etc/hostname, /etc/hosts and /etc/resolv.conf come from? → files in its folder under /var/lib/docker/containers, mounted in at start
title: Logs & Files on Disk

text: What is a multi-stage build? → several `FROM` stages in one Dockerfile, a heavy stage compiles the app and the last, slim stage copies only the artifact with `COPY --from`
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: Why use it? → the final image has no compiler, source or build cache, so it is smaller and has a smaller attack surface
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: What is a distroless image? → a base with the app runtime only, no shell, no package manager, no OS tools
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: Benefits of distroless? → fewer CVEs, smaller image, an attacker who gets in has no shell or `curl` to use
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: Downsides? → no `docker exec` shell, no `RUN apt install` in the final stage, only exec-form `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`, debugging needs the `:debug` tag or an ephemeral container
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: Why did `RUN apt update` fail on a distroless base? → `RUN` starts `/bin/sh -c` and the image has no `/bin/sh`
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: How do you debug a distroless container in Kubernetes? → `kubectl debug` with an ephemeral container that shares the pod's namespaces
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: `distroless` vs `scratch` vs `alpine`? → `scratch` is empty and only fits static binaries, distroless adds CA certs, timezone data and a non-root user, `alpine` is small but has a shell and uses musl
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: How do you harden an image? → multi-stage build, minimal or distroless base, non-root `USER`, pinned versions, no secrets in `ENV`
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: What does `docker build --target` do? → builds only up to the named stage and tags that
title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless

text: What is a Linux namespace? → a kernel feature that gives a set of processes its own view of a resource (processes, network, mounts, hostname...)
title: Namespaces

text: Namespaces vs cgroups? → namespaces limit what a process can see; cgroups limit what it can use
title: Namespaces

text: Name the 7 namespaces → PID, NET, MNT, UTS, IPC, USER, CGROUP (plus TIME on newer kernels)
title: Namespaces

text: Is container root the same as host root? → by default yes; user namespace remapping or rootless Docker changes that
title: Namespaces

text: How do you get a shell in a container's network namespace from the host? → nsenter -t <pid> -n
title: Namespaces

text: Why can 10 containers all listen on port 80? → each has its own network namespace
title: Namespaces

text: What is docker0? → a Linux bridge (software switch) created by dockerd; containers plug into it via veth pairs and use 172.17.0.1 as their gateway
title: Networking

text: What is a veth pair? → a virtual cable; one end is eth0 inside the container, the other is plugged into the bridge on the host
title: Networking

text: What does -p 8080:80 mean? → host port 8080 forwards to container port 80 (HOST:CONTAINER) via an iptables DNAT rule
title: Networking

text: Why can't I reach a container without -p? → its IP is private to the host; nothing listens on the host port
title: Networking

text: Does EXPOSE publish a port? → no, it only documents it
title: Networking

text: How does a container reach the internet? → through docker0, then iptables MASQUERADE rewrites its source IP to the host's
title: Networking

text: Why can two containers use port 80 but not the same host port? → each has its own network namespace, but the host has only one of each port
title: Networking

text: Default bridge vs user-defined network? → user-defined networks have built-in DNS so containers reach each other by name
title: Networking

text: Why does a published port ignore UFW? → Docker's iptables rules are evaluated before UFW's
title: Networking

text: What is a network driver? → the type of network, i.e. how Docker wires the container: bridge, host, none, overlay, macvlan/ipvlan
title: Networking

text: Can a container on one user-defined network reach a container on another? → no, bridges are isolated by iptables; connect the container to both networks to cross
title: Networking

text: How do you add a running container to another network? → docker network connect <network> <container>; it gets a second interface (eth1)
title: Networking

text: Which DNS server do containers on a user-defined network use? → Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11
title: Networking

text: Why use names instead of container IPs? → IPs change when containers restart, names stay the same
title: Networking

text: When would you use --network host? → when the container must see or serve on the host's network directly, e.g. Node Exporter; you lose isolation and can get port conflicts
title: Networking

text: Why does docker ps show no ports in host mode? → nothing is forwarded; the app listens on the host's port directly
title: Networking

text: Why does a /16 network show 65530 available IPs with 3 containers? → 65,536 minus the network address, gateway, broadcast and the 3 containers
title: Networking

text: Volume vs bind mount? → a volume is managed by Docker and referenced by name, a bind mount maps a host path you choose. Volumes for persistent app data, bind mounts for dev code and config
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: Container was deleted and the data is gone, why? → the data was in the container's writable layer. Mount a volume on the data path
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: Does `--rm` delete a named volume? → no, only the container (and anonymous volumes). Named volumes stay until `docker volume rm`
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: How do you tell `-v` volume from bind mount? → source starting with `/` or `./` is a bind mount, a plain name is a volume
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: Why prefer `--mount` over `-v`? → it is explicit, and it errors on a missing bind source instead of creating an empty directory
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: Files written by a container show up root-owned on the host? → the container runs as root. Use `--user` with the host UID and GID
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: Where are named volumes stored on Linux? → `/var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data`, readable only by root
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: How would you back up a volume? → run a throwaway container that mounts the volume and a host folder, and `tar` the data
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: When would you use `tmpfs`? → temporary or sensitive data you don't want written to disk
title: Volumes & Bind Mounts

text: Archive vs compress → `tar` bundles, `gzip` shrinks, `zip` loses Unix metadata
title: Archiving & Backup

text: `rsync` vs `scp` → `scp` copies everything every time, `rsync` only changes + resumes
title: Archiving & Backup

text: `rsync src/` vs `rsync src` → trailing slash copies contents, no slash copies the folder itself
title: Archiving & Backup

text: `cp` → Copy | `mv` → Move/Rename | `rm` → Remove
title: Files & Directories

text: `mkdir` → Create directory | `touch` → Create file / update timestamps
title: Files & Directories

text: `find` → Search filesystem
title: Files & Directories

text: Hard vs soft link: hard shares the inode and survives deleting the original; soft has its own inode, can cross disks and point to dirs, and breaks if the target is deleted.
title: Files & Directories

text: Disk full, find big files → `find / -type f -size +100M 2>/dev/null` or `du -sh /* | sort -h`
title: Finding Files

text: Delete logs older than 7 days → `find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime +7 -delete`
title: Finding Files

text: `-exec {} \;` vs `{} +` → once per file vs once with all files
title: Finding Files

text: locate vs find → locate = fast but stale db, find = live search
title: Finding Files

text: `Ctrl-C` sends SIGINT (stop); `Ctrl-Z` sends SIGTSTP (pause, resumable with `fg`).
title: Keyboard Shortcuts

text: `sudo !!` → fastest fix for "Permission denied".
title: Keyboard Shortcuts

text: Never put passwords or tokens on the command line; they're saved in `~/.bash_history`.
title: Keyboard Shortcuts

text: Can't reach a server → `ping` (up?) → `ss` on server (listening?) → firewall/security group → DNS (`resolvectl`/`dig`)
title: Networking

text: App works on server but not from outside → bound to `127.0.0.1` not `0.0.0.0`, or port blocked
title: Networking

text: "Permissions are too open" → `chmod 600` key, `chmod 700 ~/.ssh`
title: Networking

text: Ping fails but curl works → ICMP blocked, host is fine
title: Networking

text: update vs upgrade → update = refresh list, upgrade = install new versions
title: Package Management

text: remove vs purge → purge also deletes config
title: Package Management

text: "Unable to locate package" → run `apt update`, check spelling, check repo enabled
title: Package Management

text: "Which package gave me this file?" → `dpkg -S /path`
title: Package Management

text: "Permission denied running ./script.sh" → check `x` bit (`ls -l`), `chmod +x`; run `bash script.sh` to bypass; check if the disk is mounted `noexec`.
title: Permissions

text: Even root can't run a file with no `x` bit at all; root can read/write anything.
title: Permissions

text: SSH says "permissions are too open" → `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, `chmod 700 ~/.ssh`.
title: Permissions

text: Deleting a file is controlled by the directory's `w`, not the file's.
title: Permissions

text: Directory `x` = permission to enter/access; `r` = permission to list names.
title: Permissions

text: `/tmp` is 1777: everyone writes, sticky bit stops users deleting each other's files.
title: Permissions

text: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL → TERM lets the program clean up (close files, release locks, finish writes); KILL can't be caught, so data or locks can be left broken. Always TERM first.
title: Processes

text: Zombie → finished process whose parent hasn't read its exit status. `kill -9` does nothing; deal with the parent.
title: Processes

text: `D` state process won't die even with `kill -9` → it's stuck on I/O (often a disk or NFS issue).
title: Processes

text: "Server is slow" → `top` (load average, CPU vs `nproc`, memory, swap) → sort by `P`/`M` → `ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head` → check that process's logs.
title: Processes

text: "Port 8080 already in use" → `sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8080` → find the PID → `kill` it or stop its service.
title: Processes

text: PID 1 is systemd; it starts services and adopts orphans.
title: Processes

text: Redirection is set up by the shell before the command starts.
title: Redirection & Pipes

text: Pipe connects stdout → stdin; stderr needs 2>&1.
title: Redirection & Pipes

text: `> f 2>&1` works, `2>&1 > f` doesn't (left to right).
title: Redirection & Pipes

text: `sudo echo > /etc/f` fails; use `| sudo tee`.
title: Redirection & Pipes

text: Never redirect into the file you're reading.
title: Redirection & Pipes

text: The shell expands the command first; the program never sees `*`, `~` or `$var`.
title: Expansion & Quoting

text: Globbing is done by the shell → why `find . -name *.txt` breaks; quote it: `find . -name "*.txt"`
title: Expansion & Quoting

text: Single vs double quotes: single = fully literal, double = variables still expand.
title: Expansion & Quoting

text: Always quote variables (`"$var"`) to avoid word splitting on spaces.
title: Expansion & Quoting

text: Brace expansion makes names; globbing matches existing files.
title: Expansion & Quoting

text: What happens on `systemctl start x` → systemd reads `x.service`, starts dependencies, runs `ExecStart` as a new process, tracks its PID, logs to the journal, and restarts it if `Restart=` is set
title: systemd & Services

text: start vs enable → now vs at boot | `enable` creates a symlink in the `.wants` folder
title: systemd & Services

text: Service won't start after reboot → `is-enabled` (enabled?) → `status` → `journalctl -u` → path/permissions
title: systemd & Services

text: Edited a unit file and nothing changed → forgot `daemon-reload`
title: systemd & Services

text: How to exit vim without saving → `Esc` then `:q!`
title: vi / vim

text: Edit a config on a server with no nano → `vim`, `i`, edit, `Esc`, `:wq`
title: vi / vim

text: `type` vs `which` → type knows aliases/builtins/functions; which only finds files in $PATH.
title: Working with Commands

text: "Command not found" → check `echo $PATH`, `which cmd`, whether it's installed, and whether you need `./` for a file in the current directory.
title: Working with Commands

text: "Wrong version runs" → `type -a cmd` shows every match; the first one wins.
title: Working with Commands

text: How does Terraform authenticate to AWS? → the provider uses the standard AWS credential chain: provider config, env vars, shared credentials/config files, then instance or container roles
title: AWS Auth & S3

text: Authentication vs authorization? → authentication proves identity (keys, SSO, role); authorization is what IAM policies allow that identity to do
title: AWS Auth & S3

text: Why not hardcode access keys in the provider block? → they end up in Git; use profiles, SSO or roles, and OIDC in CI
title: AWS Auth & S3

text: How do you check which AWS account Terraform will use? → `aws sts get-caller-identity`
title: AWS Auth & S3

text: Why must S3 bucket names be globally unique? → buckets share one global namespace and are addressed by DNS names like `bucket.s3.amazonaws.com`
title: AWS Auth & S3

text: Why are versioning and encryption separate resources from `aws_s3_bucket`? → since AWS provider v4 each bucket setting is its own resource, so it can be managed independently
title: AWS Auth & S3

text: How do you create a dependency between two resources? → reference an attribute of one in the other (implicit); use `depends_on` only for hidden dependencies
title: AWS Auth & S3

text: Does the order of resource blocks matter? → no, Terraform builds a dependency graph from references
title: AWS Auth & S3

text: Is an S3 bucket inside a VPC? → no, S3 is a regional service; a VPC reaches it over the internet or through a VPC endpoint
title: AWS Auth & S3

text: Resource vs data source? → resource creates and manages infra; data source only reads existing infra
title: HCL Syntax

text: `count` vs `for_each`? → `count` indexes by number so removing a middle item recreates later ones; `for_each` keys by name so changes stay targeted
title: HCL Syntax

text: How does Terraform decide creation order? → builds a dependency graph from references; `depends_on` for hidden dependencies
title: HCL Syntax

text: When do you need `depends_on`? → when one resource relies on another without referencing any of its attributes, e.g. an app needing an IAM policy attached first
title: HCL Syntax

text: Variable precedence? → `-var` / `-var-file` > `*.auto.tfvars` > `terraform.tfvars` > `TF_VAR_` env vars > `default`
title: HCL Syntax

text: Does `sensitive = true` keep a value out of state? → no, only out of CLI output; state still has it in plain text
title: HCL Syntax

text: What does `create_before_destroy` do? → builds the replacement first, then deletes the old one, avoiding downtime
title: HCL Syntax

text: Variable vs local? → variable is an input set from outside; local is a computed value used inside the module
title: HCL Syntax

text: What is IaC and why use it? → managing infra through versioned code instead of manual setup; repeatable, reviewable, consistent across environments
title: IaC & Terraform

text: Terraform vs Ansible? → Terraform provisions infrastructure (declarative, stateful), Ansible configures software on machines (procedural, agentless); commonly used together
title: IaC & Terraform

text: Declarative vs imperative? → declarative describes the end state and the tool works out the steps; imperative lists the steps
title: IaC & Terraform

text: What is the Terraform state file? → JSON mapping of resources in code to real objects; used to calculate diffs; may contain secrets, so store it remotely and encrypted
title: IaC & Terraform

text: What does `terraform plan` do? → compares code with state and real infra, shows what would be created, changed or destroyed without changing anything
title: IaC & Terraform

text: What does `-/+` in a plan mean? → the resource will be destroyed and recreated, so check it for data loss
title: IaC & Terraform

text: Is Terraform open source? → not since 2023 (BSL licence); OpenTofu is the open-source fork
title: IaC & Terraform

text: What is drift? → real infra changed outside Terraform; `plan` detects it and `apply` brings it back to the code
title: IaC & Terraform

text: What does `create_before_destroy` do? → builds the replacement first and then destroys the old one → avoids downtime
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: Gotcha with `create_before_destroy`? → both resources exist at once → a fixed unique name collides → use `name_prefix`
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: What does `prevent_destroy` do? → makes Terraform error on any plan that would destroy the resource
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: Does `prevent_destroy` protect you if the block is deleted from the code? → no → the guard is gone with the block
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: Does `prevent_destroy` block replacement? → yes → replacement destroys the old resource
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: What does `ignore_changes` do? → Terraform skips drift on the listed attributes → it also ignores your own config edits to them
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: Real use of `ignore_changes`? → ASG `desired_capacity` managed by autoscaling, tags added by other tools
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: `precondition` vs `postcondition`? → precondition checks inputs before creation, postcondition checks the result after with `self`
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: Variable `validation` vs `precondition`? → `validation` checks one variable, `precondition` can check across variables, data sources and resources
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: When does a postcondition fail without creating anything? → when the attribute is known at plan time
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: What does `replace_triggered_by` do? → replaces a resource when another resource or attribute changes, even if its own arguments did not
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: How do you trigger replacement from a variable change? → put the variable in a `terraform_data` input and reference it in `replace_triggered_by`
title: Lifecycle Rules

text: What is a meta-argument? → an argument available on any resource regardless of provider, e.g. `count`, `for_each`, `depends_on`, `provider`, `lifecycle`
title: Meta-Arguments

text: What is `count.index`? → the zero-based index of the current copy of a resource that uses `count`
title: Meta-Arguments

text: `count` vs `for_each`? → `count` identifies copies by position, `for_each` by key → prefer `for_each` for distinct resources
title: Meta-Arguments

text: Why is `for_each` safer than `count` when removing an item? → with `count` the indexes shift and later resources get destroyed and recreated, with `for_each` only the removed key is touched
title: Meta-Arguments

text: What types does `for_each` accept? → a map or a set of strings, so wrap a list in `toset()`
title: Meta-Arguments

text: What are `each.key` and `each.value` for a set? → both are the item itself
title: Meta-Arguments

text: What happens with `count = 4` on a 3-item list? → plan fails with `Invalid index`, nothing is created
title: Meta-Arguments

text: Can you use `count` and `for_each` on the same resource? → no
title: Meta-Arguments

text: When do you need `depends_on`? → only for hidden dependencies, where B needs A but does not reference any of its attributes
title: Meta-Arguments

text: What does `prevent_destroy` do? → makes Terraform error on any plan that would destroy the resource
title: Meta-Arguments

text: What is a Terraform provider? → a plugin that implements resources and data sources for an API and translates HCL into API calls
title: Providers & Versioning

text: Why pin provider versions? → major versions have breaking changes; pinning keeps plans reproducible across machines and CI
title: Providers & Versioning

text: What does `~> 6.1` allow? → `>= 6.1, < 7.0`, any 6.x from 6.1 up
title: Providers & Versioning

text: What does `~> 6.1.1` allow? → `>= 6.1.1, < 6.2.0`, patch releases only
title: Providers & Versioning

text: What is `.terraform.lock.hcl`? → records the exact provider versions and checksums chosen by `init`; commit it so everyone uses the same build
title: Providers & Versioning

text: Constraint vs lock file? → constraint is the allowed range, the lock is the exact version picked inside it; `init -upgrade` moves it
title: Providers & Versioning

text: How do you deploy to two regions in one config? → a second `provider` block with `alias`, then `provider = aws.<alias>` on the resources
title: Providers & Versioning

text: Where should AWS credentials come from? → env vars, an AWS profile or an IAM role / OIDC; never hardcoded in `.tf` files
title: Providers & Versioning

text: Terraform core vs provider version? → core is the CLI binary pinned by `required_version`; providers are separate plugins pinned in `required_providers`, each with its own releases
title: Providers & Versioning

text: What is the Terraform state file? → JSON mapping resources in code to real infrastructure, used to calculate diffs; may contain secrets
title: State & Remote Backend

text: Why use a remote backend? → shared state for teams and CI, locking, encryption, versioned backups, no secrets in Git
title: State & Remote Backend

text: How does S3 native state locking work? → Terraform creates a `.tflock` object with a conditional write (`If-None-Match`); if it already exists S3 returns 412 and the second run fails
title: State & Remote Backend

text: Do you still need DynamoDB for locking? → no, from Terraform 1.10 `use_lockfile = true` locks with S3 alone; DynamoDB locking is deprecated
title: State & Remote Backend

text: What happens if the state file is lost? → Terraform no longer knows what it manages; recover from a bucket version, or `terraform import` the resources back
title: State & Remote Backend

text: How do you handle a stuck lock? → confirm no run is active, then `terraform force-unlock <lock-id>`
title: State & Remote Backend

text: Can you use variables in the backend block? → no, the backend is configured before variables are evaluated; use `-backend-config` for dynamic values
title: State & Remote Backend

text: How do you separate environments? → different state keys (`dev/`, `prod/`) or separate backends, so a change in one can't affect the other
title: State & Remote Backend

text: `state rm` vs `destroy`? → `state rm` forgets the resource but leaves it running; `destroy` deletes the real resource
title: State & Remote Backend

text: Two engineers apply different code against the same state, what happens? → locking serializes the runs but doesn't merge code; the second plan destroys whatever its code lacks, so use PRs and CI-only applies
title: State & Remote Backend

text: What does `terraform import` do? → adds an existing real resource to state under an address in your code; it writes state only, so the matching resource block must exist first
title: State & Remote Backend

text: How do you bring console-created infra into Terraform? → write matching resource blocks (or use an `import` block with `plan -generate-config-out`), import, then adjust code until `plan` shows no changes
title: State & Remote Backend

text: You renamed a resource in code and the plan wants to recreate it, what do you do? → `terraform state mv <old> <new>` so the existing object is tracked under the new address
title: State & Remote Backend

text: You ran `state rm` by mistake, how do you recover? → don't apply; find the real ID and `terraform import` it back, then confirm `plan` shows no changes
title: State & Remote Backend

text: Does `destroy` delete the state file? → no, it deletes the resources and leaves an empty state with a higher serial
title: State & Remote Backend

text: Why declare types on variables? → bad input fails at `plan` with a clear message instead of a confusing provider error mid-apply
title: Type Constraints

text: List vs set? → list is ordered, allows duplicates and has index access; set is unordered, unique and has no index
title: Type Constraints

text: Why use a set instead of a list? → `for_each` needs stable keys; reordering causes no diff; duplicates are impossible
title: Type Constraints

text: Why is `for_each` preferred over `count`? → `count` keys by index, so removing a middle item shifts and recreates later resources; `for_each` keys by value, so only the removed one is destroyed
title: Type Constraints

text: Can you index a set? → no, `Invalid index`; use `tolist()` or loop over it with `for_each`
title: Type Constraints

text: `each.key` vs `each.value`? → same for a set; for a map, key is the map key and value is its value
title: Type Constraints

text: Map vs object? → map has any keys with one value type; object has fixed field names with their own types
title: Type Constraints

text: Tuple vs object? → both have a fixed shape with mixed types; tuple by position, object by name; object is more readable and supports `optional()`
title: Type Constraints

text: What does `map(any)` do with `{ a = "x", b = 5 }`? → picks one type for all values, so `5` becomes `"5"`
title: Type Constraints

text: How do you make an object field optional? → `optional(type, default)`, Terraform 1.3+
title: Type Constraints

text: How do you restrict a variable to allowed values? → `validation` block with `contains([...], var.x)` and an `error_message`
title: Type Constraints

text: What's the most common real-world `for_each` type? → `map(object({...}))`: many items, each with the same shape
title: Type Constraints

text: Does `terraform validate` catch a wrong value like a region in `instance_type`? → no, it checks syntax and types only; the AWS API rejects it at `apply`
title: Type Constraints

text: Variable vs local? → a variable is an input set from outside per run; a local is a value computed inside the module and can't be overridden
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: Why can't a variable's default use another variable? → defaults must be fixed values; computed values belong in locals
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: What is the variable precedence order? → default, then `TF_VAR_` env vars, `terraform.tfvars`, `terraform.tfvars.json`, `*.auto.tfvars` in alphabetical order, and `-var` / `-var-file` on the command line last and strongest
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: `terraform.tfvars` vs `prod.tfvars`? → `terraform.tfvars` and `*.auto.tfvars` load automatically; any other name loads only with `-var-file`
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: How do you pass secrets to Terraform? → `TF_VAR_` env vars or a secrets manager, mark the variable `sensitive = true`; the value still lands in state, so the state must be protected
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: How do you enforce common tags on all resources? → a `common_tags` local merged into each resource's tags with `merge()`, or the AWS provider's `default_tags` block
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: list vs set vs tuple? → list is ordered with duplicates, set is unordered and unique, tuple has a fixed length with a type per position
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: map vs object? → map has any keys with one value type; object has fixed keys with their own types
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: What are outputs used for? → showing values after apply, feeding scripts via `-raw` / `-json`, and passing values between modules and stacks
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: Does `sensitive = true` hide a value from state? → no, only from CLI output
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: How do you get unique S3 bucket names? → add a suffix from `random_string` (stored in state so it stays stable) or include account and region in the name
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs

text: Is changing a variable enough to create a separate prod environment? → no, with the same backend key it modifies the same resources; prod needs its own state
title: Variables, Locals & Outputs
